question: Who promoted the worship of God in Punjab, India as Nirankar (Formless)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Baba Dayal Das.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Baba Dayal Das (1783–1855) founded the Nirankari movement in Punjab, preaching the worship of God as Nirankar — the Formless One. (निरंकार — निराकार ईश्वर)

• He opposed idol worship, ritualism and Brahmanical ceremonies, and urged Sikhs to return to the pure teachings of Guru Nanak.

• The movement began at Rawalpindi (now in Pakistan) and is regarded as one of the earliest socio-religious reform movements in 19th-century Punjab.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Guru Gobind Singh — the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib in 1699.

• Baba Ram Singh — founder of the Namdhari (Kuka) movement (1857), known for its early use of boycott and non-cooperation.

• Maharaja Ranjit Singh — the “Lion of Punjab”, founder of the Sikh Empire with its capital at Lahore (ruled 1801–1839).

NOTE

• Reform movements to remember: Brahmo Samaj — Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1828); Arya Samaj — Swami Dayanand Saraswati (1875); Prarthana Samaj — Atmaram Pandurang (1867).

• The Nirankari and Namdhari movements are both Punjab-based Sikh reform streams frequently asked in SSC exams.

question: Who among the following is a Sarangi player?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ustad Shakoor Khan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Ustad Shakoor Khan was a celebrated Indian sarangi maestro of the Hindustani classical tradition. (सारंगी — तारवाद्य)

• The sarangi is a bowed, short-necked string instrument whose tone is said to resemble the human voice; it is widely used to accompany khayal and thumri singing.

• Other renowned sarangi players include Pandit Ram Narayan and Ustad Sultan Khan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Pandit Kishan (Krishna) Maharaj — a legendary tabla player of the Benaras gharana, awarded the Padma Vibhushan.

• Sandeep Das — a tabla exponent and Grammy-winning member of the Silk Road Ensemble.

• Anuradha Paudwal — a well-known Indian playback singer, not an instrumentalist.

NOTE

• Instrument–artist pairs often asked: Sitar — Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan; Sarod — Amjad Ali Khan, Ali Akbar Khan; Shehnai — Bismillah Khan; Flute — Hariprasad Chaurasia; Santoor — Shivkumar Sharma; Violin — L. Subramaniam.

question: What does the Surrogacy (Regulation) Bill, 2016 prohibit?
option_1: Women aged between 23 to 50 as surrogates
solution_text:
The correct answer is Commercial Surrogacy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Surrogacy (Regulation) Bill, 2016 prohibits commercial surrogacy and permits only altruistic surrogacy, in which the surrogate mother receives no monetary compensation beyond medical expenses and insurance cover. (वाणिज्यिक सरोगेसी पर प्रतिबंध)

• The Bill was introduced to stop the exploitation of poor women and the growth of “rent-a-womb” commercial clinics in India.

• It provided for the establishment of a National Surrogacy Board and State Surrogacy Boards for regulation.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Bill allowed women aged between 25 and 35 years to act as surrogates — so an age band of 23 to 50 is not what is prohibited.

• A surrogate had to be a married woman with a child of her own, so married women were in fact permitted, not banned.

• The law was finally enacted as the Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021, which came into force on 25 January 2022.

NOTE

• Related law: the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021 regulates ART clinics and banks.

• Intending couples must be Indian, legally married, and hold a certificate of essentiality and certificate of eligibility.

question: A report named “Payments Vision 2025” is released by which institution?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Reserve Bank of India.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Payments Vision 2025 was released by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in June 2022, prepared by its Department of Payment and Settlement Systems. (भुगतान दृष्टिकोण 2025)

• Its core theme is “E-Payments for Everyone, Everywhere, Everytime (4Es)”, aiming at a highly digital, cash-lite society.

• Goals included a 3x increase in digital payment transactions, growth of UPI at 50% CAGR, and a rise in debit card and PPI transactions.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• RBI was established on 1 April 1935 on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission; it was nationalised in 1949. Headquarters: Mumbai.

• NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission and publishes the SDG India Index and India Innovation Index.

• The Ministry of Finance presents the Union Budget and the Economic Survey (prepared by the Chief Economic Adviser).

NOTE

• Other RBI payment initiatives: UPI (2016), NEFT, RTGS, Bharat Bill Payment System, NUE framework and e-RUPI.

• RBI’s payment systems are operated largely through the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), set up in 2008.

question: During October – November, the apparent movement of sun is towards the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is South.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• After the summer solstice (21 June), when the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, its apparent path begins shifting southward. (सूर्य का दक्षिणायन)

• Therefore during October – November the Sun’s apparent movement is towards the south, reaching the Tropic of Capricorn on 22 December (winter solstice).

• This southward journey is called Dakshinayan, while the northward journey from 22 December to 21 June is called Uttarayan.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• The Sun’s apparent north–south movement is caused by the inclination of the Earth’s axis at 23½° to the plane of its orbit, combined with revolution — not by any real motion of the Sun.

• On the equinoxes — 21 March and 23 September — the Sun is vertically overhead at the Equator and day and night are equal everywhere.

• The withdrawal of the South-West monsoon in October–November is linked to this southward shift, giving India the retreating monsoon season.

NOTE

• 21 June — longest day in the Northern Hemisphere; 22 December — shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere.

• The Sun is never overhead beyond 23½°N and 23½°S, which is why the region between the tropics is called the torrid zone.

question: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought between ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Marathas and Afghans.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Third Battle of Panipat was fought on 14 January 1761 between the Marathas, led by Sadashivrao Bhau, and the Afghan forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani). (पानीपत का तृतीय युद्ध)

• Abdali was supported by Najib-ud-Daula of Rohilkhand and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh; the Marathas were decisively defeated.

• Vishwasrao, son of Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao, was killed, and the defeat halted Maratha expansion in North India, indirectly aiding the rise of the British.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• First Battle of Panipat (1526) — Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi, founding the Mughal Empire; first major use of field artillery and tulughma tactics in India.

• Second Battle of Panipat (1556) — Akbar’s forces under Bairam Khan defeated Hemu (Hemchandra Vikramaditya).

• Panipat lies in present-day Haryana, on the historic route from the north-west into the Gangetic plain.

NOTE

• Other decisive battles: Battle of Plassey (1757) — Clive vs Siraj-ud-Daulah; Battle of Buxar (1764) — British vs Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II; Battle of Talikota (1565) — end of Vijayanagara power.

question: ‘The Race of My Life: An Autobiography’ is written by which famous athlete?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Milkha Singh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• ‘The Race of My Life: An Autobiography’ was written by the legendary sprinter Milkha Singh along with his daughter Sonia Sanwalka. (मिल्खा सिंह — ‘द फ्लाइंग सिख’)

• Milkha Singh, known as the “Flying Sikh”, won gold in the 400 m at the 1958 Commonwealth Games in Cardiff — India’s first individual athletics gold there.

• He famously finished fourth in the 400 m final at the 1960 Rome Olympics, narrowly missing a medal; the book inspired the film Bhaag Milkha Bhaag (2013).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• PV Sindhu — badminton star, Olympic silver (Rio 2016) and bronze (Tokyo 2020), and World Champion in 2019.

• Nitender Singh Rawat — Indian long-distance runner and marathoner.

• Milkha Singh was awarded the Padma Shri in 1959 and also won gold at the 1958 and 1962 Asian Games.

NOTE

• Sports autobiographies frequently asked: Playing It My Way — Sachin Tendulkar; Ace Against Odds — Sania Mirza; Unbreakable — Mary Kom; Straight from the Heart — Kapil Dev; A Shot at History — Abhinav Bindra.

question: The star athlete Jwala Gutta is associated with which sport?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Badminton.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Jwala Gutta is a former Indian badminton player, famous as a doubles specialist. (बैडमिंटन)

• With Ashwini Ponnappa she won a bronze medal at the 2011 BWF World Championships — India’s first women’s doubles medal at the Worlds — and gold at the 2010 Commonwealth Games, Delhi.

• She also partnered V. Diju in mixed doubles and was awarded the Arjuna Award in 2011.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Indian table tennis names: Achanta Sharath Kamal, Manika Batra, Sathiyan Gnanasekaran.

• Indian squash names: Saurav Ghosal, Dipika Pallikal, Joshna Chinappa.

• Indian lawn tennis names: Leander Paes, Mahesh Bhupathi, Sania Mirza, Rohan Bopanna.

NOTE

• Badminton terms: smash, drop shot, deuce, let, service court, shuttlecock.

• Major badminton trophies: Thomas Cup (men’s team — won by India in 2022), Uber Cup (women’s team), Sudirman Cup (mixed team).

question: The bodies of living organism are made of tiny units called ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is cells.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life; all living organisms are made up of one or more cells. (कोशिका — जीवन की मूल इकाई)

• The cell was discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665 while examining a thin slice of cork; Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

• The Cell Theory was proposed by Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839), and extended by Rudolf Virchow (1855) with “Omnis cellula-e cellula” — all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Genes are segments of DNA on chromosomes that carry hereditary information; the term was coined by Wilhelm Johannsen.

• Centrioles are cylindrical organelles found in animal cells that help form the spindle fibres during cell division.

• Budding is a mode of asexual reproduction seen in yeast and *Hydra*.

NOTE

• Largest cell — ostrich egg; longest cell — nerve cell; smallest cell — *Mycoplasma*.

• Cell organelles: Mitochondria — powerhouse; Ribosome — protein factory; Lysosome — suicidal bag; Golgi body — packaging; Chloroplast — photosynthesis.

question: Volleyball is played by two teams of ______ players each.
solution_text:
The correct answer is six.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Volleyball is played between two teams of six players each on court, separated by a net. (वॉलीबॉल — प्रत्येक टीम में 6 खिलाड़ी)

• The game was invented by William G. Morgan in 1895 in Massachusetts, USA, originally called “Mintonette”.

• The governing body is the FIVB (Fédération Internationale de Volleyball), founded in 1947, headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Basketball and Kabaddi have five and seven players per side respectively; Kho-Kho and Handball have nine and seven.

• A standard volleyball court measures 18 m × 9 m; net height is 2.43 m for men and 2.24 m for women.

• A set is won at 25 points (with a two-point margin); the deciding fifth set is played to 15 points.

NOTE

• Volleyball terms: smash, spike, service ace, block, libero, deuce, dig, set-up.

• Players per side: Cricket 11, Football 11, Hockey 11, Polo 4, Water Polo 7, Baseball 9, Rugby 15.

question: What is the characteristic of isotopes?
option_2: Same atomic number and different mass number
option_3: Same atomic number and same mass number
solution_text:
The correct answer is Same atomic number and different mass number.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number (same number of protons) but a different mass number because they contain different numbers of neutrons. (समस्थानिक)

• Examples: Hydrogen — protium (¹H), deuterium (²H), tritium (³H); Carbon — ¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C; Chlorine — ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl.

• Since chemical properties depend on the number of electrons/protons, isotopes have identical chemical properties but different physical properties.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Isobars — atoms of different elements with different atomic numbers but the same mass number, e.g. ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰K and ⁴⁰Ca.

• Isotones — atoms having the same number of neutrons but different atomic and mass numbers, e.g. ³⁶S, ³⁷Cl, ³⁸Ar.

• Atoms with the same number of protons and neutrons are simply the same nuclide, not isotopes.

NOTE

• Uses of isotopes: U-235 in nuclear reactors; Co-60 in cancer therapy; I-131 for thyroid disorders; C-14 for radio-carbon dating.

• Mass number (A) = protons + neutrons; Atomic number (Z) = number of protons.

question: The long term objective of National Population Policy (NPP) 2000 is to achieve a stable population by ______ with sustainable economic growth, social development and environmental protection.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2045.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The National Population Policy (NPP), 2000 set as its long-term objective the achievement of a stable population by 2045, at a level consistent with sustainable economic growth, social development and environmental protection. (राष्ट्रीय जनसंख्या नीति 2000)

• Its medium-term objective was to bring the Total Fertility Rate (TFR) to the replacement level of 2.1 by 2010.

• The immediate objective was to address unmet needs for contraception, health-care infrastructure and trained health personnel.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• NPP 2000 also aimed at universal immunisation, reducing Infant Mortality Rate below 30 per 1000 live births and Maternal Mortality Ratio below 100 per lakh live births.

• It promoted the small family norm, delaying the age at marriage of girls, and achieving 80% institutional deliveries.

• India’s first official family planning programme was launched in 1952, making it the first country in the world to do so.

NOTE

• The National Commission on Population was constituted in May 2000, chaired by the Prime Minister.

• As per NFHS-5 (2019–21), India’s TFR has fallen to 2.0, below the replacement level.

question: Hauz-i-Sultani was constructed by ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Iltutmish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Hauz-i-Sultani, also known as Hauz-i-Shamsi, was a large water reservoir built by Shams-ud-din Iltutmish around 1230 AD at Mehrauli, Delhi. (हौज़-ए-शम्सी — जलाशय)

• Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236) was the real consolidator of the Delhi Sultanate and belonged to the Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty.

• He completed the Qutub Minar begun by Qutub-ud-din Aibak, introduced the silver tanka and copper jital, and organised the nobility known as the Chahalgani (Turkan-i-Chahalgani).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Sikandar Lodi founded the city of Agra in 1504 and wrote poetry under the pen name Gulrukhi.

• Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 and wrote the Baburnama in Turkish.

• Akbar built Fatehpur Sikri, the Buland Darwaza and the Ibadat Khana, and promulgated Din-i-Ilahi in 1582.

NOTE

• Other tanks/reservoirs: Hauz-i-Alai (Hauz Khas) — Alauddin Khilji; Hauz-i-Shamsi — Iltutmish.

• Iltutmish received a mansur (letter of investiture) from the Caliph of Baghdad in 1229, giving legal status to the Delhi Sultanate.

question: Which type of farming is practiced to meet the needs of the farmer’s family?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Subsistence farming.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Subsistence farming is practised on small landholdings with simple tools and family labour, primarily to meet the needs of the farmer’s own family. (निर्वाह कृषि)

• Output is consumed locally, with little or no surplus for sale; productivity is low due to limited use of machinery, fertilisers and irrigation.

• It is of two types — primitive (shifting) subsistence farming such as Jhum in North-East India, and intensive subsistence farming practised in densely populated monsoon regions.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Commercial farming is carried out on a large scale for sale in the market, using HYV seeds, fertilisers and machinery; plantation farming is a type of commercial farming.

• Pisciculture is the rearing of fish, and sericulture is the rearing of silkworms for raw silk.

• Other related terms: Apiculture — bee-keeping; Horticulture — fruits and vegetables; Viticulture — grapes; Floriculture — flowers.

NOTE

• Shifting cultivation has local names: Jhum (North-East India), Podu (Andhra Pradesh), Kumari (Western Ghats), Bewar/Dahiya (Madhya Pradesh), Milpa (Mexico), Ladang (Indonesia).

question: Which of the following articles of the Indian constitution is related to “Organisation of village panchayats”?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Article 40.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Article 40 of the Indian Constitution directs the State to organise village panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary to function as units of self-government. (ग्राम पंचायतों का संगठन)

• It is a Directive Principle of State Policy (Part IV) and reflects the Gandhian ideal of village self-rule.

• Article 40 was given practical effect by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992, which added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects), and came into force on 24 April 1993.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Article 41 — right to work, to education and to public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.

• Article 42 — provision for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.

• Article 43 — living wage, decent standard of life and promotion of cottage industries.

NOTE

• The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system; Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 Oct 1959) was the first state to implement it, followed by Andhra Pradesh.

• The 74th Amendment Act, 1992 dealt with municipalities (Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule with 18 subjects).

question: Who, with the help of Kautilya, overthrew Dhanananda, the last Nanda ruler?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chandragupta Maurya.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Chandragupta Maurya, with the guidance of his mentor Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta), overthrew Dhanananda, the last ruler of the Nanda dynasty, around 322/321 BCE and founded the Mauryan Empire. (मौर्य साम्राज्य की स्थापना)

• Kautilya authored the Arthashastra, a classic treatise on statecraft, economy and administration.

• Chandragupta defeated Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE); Seleucus sent Megasthenes as ambassador, who wrote Indica. He later embraced Jainism under Bhadrabahu and is said to have died at Shravanabelagola.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Kalashoka was a Shishunaga ruler during whose reign the Second Buddhist Council was held at Vaishali (383 BCE).

• Ashoka (268–232 BCE), grandson of Chandragupta, fought the Kalinga War (261 BCE) and spread Buddhism through rock and pillar edicts.

• Akbar was a Mughal emperor (1556–1605), unrelated to the Mauryan period.

NOTE

• Mauryan rulers in order: Chandragupta Maurya → Bindusara (Amitraghata) → Ashoka; the last ruler Brihadratha was killed by Pushyamitra Shunga (185 BCE).

• The Lion Capital of Sarnath, built by Ashoka, is India’s National Emblem.

question: Who built the Red Fort in Delhi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shah Jahan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Delhi was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan; construction began in 1638 and was completed in 1648, when he shifted his capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad. (लाल क़िला)

• It is built of red sandstone; its chief architect was Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, who also designed the Taj Mahal.

• The Red Fort was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007, and it is from its ramparts that the Prime Minister hoists the national flag on Independence Day.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 after the First Battle of Panipat.

• Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi was built by his widow Hamida Banu Begum and is called the precursor of the Taj Mahal.

• Jahangir patronised painting; his major architectural work is the tomb of Akbar at Sikandra (completed by him).

NOTE

• Shah Jahan’s other works: Taj Mahal, Jama Masjid (Delhi), Moti Masjid (Agra Fort), Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus).

• Inside the Red Fort: Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Rang Mahal, Moti Masjid (built by Aurangzeb).

question: Angela Merkel who recently won UN refugee prize is ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Former German Chancellor.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Angela Merkel, the former Chancellor of Germany (2005–2021), was awarded the UNHCR Nansen Refugee Award in 2022. (नानसेन शरणार्थी पुरस्कार)

• She was honoured for her leadership and moral courage in allowing more than 1.2 million refugees and asylum-seekers into Germany during the crisis of 2015–2016.

• She was Germany’s first woman Chancellor and was succeeded by Olaf Scholz in December 2021.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Filippo Grandi has been the UN High Commissioner for Refugees since 2016; UNHCR was established in 1950 and is headquartered in Geneva.

• António Guterres (Portugal) is the Secretary-General of the United Nations since 2017; he himself served as UN High Commissioner for Refugees earlier.

• Volodymyr Zelenskyy is the President of Ukraine.

NOTE

• The Nansen Refugee Award is named after Fridtjof Nansen, the first League of Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Nobel Peace Prize winner (1922).

• UNHCR won the Nobel Peace Prize twice — in 1954 and 1981; World Refugee Day is observed on 20 June.

question: Which of the following is used as an antacid to neutralize stomach acidity?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Magnesium Hydroxide.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Magnesium hydroxide — Mg(OH)₂, popularly called milk of magnesia, is a mild base used as an antacid to neutralise excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. (प्रतिअम्ल)

• The neutralisation reaction is: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O, which relieves acidity and indigestion.

• Other common antacids are sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and aluminium hydroxide.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Iodoform (CHI₃) is a yellow crystalline solid used as an antiseptic.

• Morphine is an analgesic (pain-killer) and narcotic obtained from opium.

• Chlorine is used as a disinfectant for water treatment and as a bleaching agent.

NOTE

• Common chemicals: NaHCO₃ — baking soda; Na₂CO₃·10H₂O — washing soda; CaOCl₂ — bleaching powder; CaSO₄·½H₂O — Plaster of Paris; Ca(OH)₂ — slaked lime.

• The pH of gastric juice is about 1.5–3.5, owing to hydrochloric acid secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach.

question: As per census 2011, which state of India has the least population?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sikkim.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per Census 2011, Sikkim is the least populous state of India, with a population of about 6.11 lakh (610,577). (सबसे कम जनसंख्या वाला राज्य)

• The most populous state is Uttar Pradesh (about 19.98 crore), followed by Maharashtra and Bihar.

• Among Union Territories, Lakshadweep had the least population (64,473) in Census 2011.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Bihar has the highest population density (1,106 persons per sq km) and the highest decadal growth rate (25.42%); Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest density (17).

• Kerala has the highest literacy rate (94%) and the highest sex ratio (1084 females per 1000 males).

• Chhattisgarh had a population of about 2.55 crore in 2011.

NOTE

• Census 2011 was the 15th national census and the 7th since Independence; its motto was “Our Census, Our Future”.

• India’s population in 2011: 121.09 crore; sex ratio 943; literacy 74.04%; Nagaland was the only state with a negative growth rate.

question: Dhangar dance comes from the Dhangar community of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Goa.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Dhangar dance is a folk dance of the Dhangar community — shepherds/cattle-herders — of Goa. (धनगर नृत्य — गोवा)

• It is performed mainly during Navratri, over several nights, in honour of Lord Krishna (Birobha), with dancers in colourful costumes moving to the beat of drums.

• The performers wear dhotis and turbans and carry a cloth, dancing in a circular formation to devotional songs called ovis.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Other Goan folk dances: Fugdi, Dekhni, Mando, Ghode Modni, Corridinho, Talgadi, Shigmo.

• Andhra Pradesh folk/classical forms: Kuchipudi (classical), Vilasini Natyam, Burrakatha.

• Gujarat — Garba, Dandiya Raas, Bhavai; Tamil Nadu — Bharatanatyam (classical), Karagattam, Kummi, Kolattam.

NOTE

• Folk dances often asked: Bihu — Assam; Chhau — Jharkhand/Odisha/West Bengal; Ghoomar — Rajasthan; Lavani — Maharashtra; Bhangra/Giddha — Punjab; Rouf — Jammu & Kashmir.

• Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule on 19 December 1961 and became a full state on 30 May 1987.

question: Change in the inventory of a firm is treated as ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Investment.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In national income accounting, the change in the stock of inventory of a firm is treated as investment — specifically inventory investment. (माल-सूची निवेश)

• Inventory includes stocks of raw materials, semi-finished goods and unsold finished goods held by a firm.

• Gross investment = Fixed investment + Inventory investment. A rise in inventory is positive investment; a fall is negative inventory investment.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Disinvestment in general economics means the sale of the government’s stake in a public-sector undertaking, or a fall in the capital stock.

• Inventory is shown as a current asset in a firm’s balance sheet, but the change in it during a year is counted as investment in GDP.

• Investment that occurs unplanned because goods remain unsold is called unintended (unplanned) inventory accumulation.

NOTE

• GDP by expenditure = C + I + G + (X − M), where I includes inventory investment.

• Net investment = Gross investment − Depreciation; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.

question: Which of the following ocean is the smallest in the world?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arctic Ocean.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world’s oceans, covering about 1.4 crore sq km (14 million sq km). (आर्कटिक महासागर — सबसे छोटा)

• It lies around the North Pole, largely covered by sea ice, and is bordered by Russia, Canada, Greenland, Norway and the USA (Alaska).

• It is connected to the Atlantic by the Greenland Sea and to the Pacific by the Bering Strait.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Pacific Ocean — the largest and deepest ocean; the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep, about 11,000 m) is the deepest point on Earth.

• Atlantic Ocean — the second largest, shaped like the letter S, and the busiest ocean for trade.

• Indian Ocean — the third largest and the only ocean named after a country; its deepest point is the Java (Sunda) Trench.

NOTE

• Oceans by size (largest → smallest): Pacific > Atlantic > Indian > Southern (Antarctic) > Arctic.

question: Bastar Dussehra is a famous festival of ________ state of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chhattisgarh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Bastar Dussehra is celebrated in the Bastar region of Chhattisgarh and is famous as one of the longest festivals in the world, lasting about 75 days. (बस्तर दशहरा)

• Unlike the rest of India, it is not linked to the Rama–Ravana legend; it is dedicated to the local deity Danteshwari Mata, the presiding goddess of the Bastar royal family.

• Its rituals include Pata Jatra, Kachhin Gaadi, Rath Parikrama (chariot procession) and Muria Durbar.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Chhattisgarh was carved out of Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 2000; capital — Raipur; its folk dances include Panthi, Raut Nacha and Karma.

• Manipur festivals: Yaoshang, Lai Haraoba, Ningol Chakouba, Cheiraoba.

• Bihar — Chhath Puja, Sonepur Mela; Arunachal Pradesh — Losar, Solung, Mopin, Nyokum.

NOTE

• Other well-known regional festivals: Hornbill — Nagaland; Bihu — Assam; Onam — Kerala; Pongal — Tamil Nadu; Hemis — Ladakh; Wangala — Meghalaya.

question: Who among the following was awarded the prestigious title of ‘Nrityacharya’ conferred by the Maharaja of Manipur?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guru Bipin Singh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Guru Bipin Singh (1918–2000) was the doyen of Manipuri dance and was conferred the prestigious title of ‘Nrityacharya’ by the Maharaja of Manipur. (नृत्याचार्य — मणिपुरी नृत्य)

• He systematised the solo repertoire of Manipuri dance and founded the Manipuri Nartanalaya in Mumbai, Kolkata and Imphal.

• His most famous disciples were the Jhaveri sisters — Nayana, Ranjana, Suverna and Darshana — who popularised Manipuri dance worldwide.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Rukmini Devi Arundale revived Bharatanatyam and founded Kalakshetra at Chennai in 1936.

• Uday Shankar was a pioneer of modern/creative dance in India, blending Indian classical and European theatrical techniques.

• Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra was the legendary exponent of Odissi, awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2000.

NOTE

• Eight classical dances: Bharatanatyam — Tamil Nadu; Kathak — Uttar Pradesh; Kathakali & Mohiniyattam — Kerala; Kuchipudi — Andhra Pradesh; Odissi — Odisha; Manipuri — Manipur; Sattriya — Assam.

• Manipuri dance forms include Raas Leela, Pung Cholom and Thang-Ta.
